wgpu_mc.notice.restart_pending: Restart Minecraft to apply the marked settings
wgpu_mc.notice.restart_applied: Restart Minecraft for these settings to take effect
wgpu_mc.option.backend.tooltip: The graphics API the renderer uses. Vulkan is the default; DirectX 12 is Windows only.
wgpu_mc.option.frames_in_flight.tooltip: How many frames the CPU may record ahead of the GPU.
wgpu_mc.option.vsync.tooltip: Sync the framerate to the display's refresh rate. Fewer torn frames, at the cost of input latency. Takes effect the moment it is applied.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain.tooltip: Draw the terrain from the meshes the Rust baker builds, in the pass Minecraft's own solid and cutout layers would have used. The translucent layer, the entities and everything after them stay Minecraft's. Takes about a second to show, because the sections are meshed again.
wgpu_mc.option.animated_textures.tooltip: Fancy: these faces sample the game's own block atlas, which is animating, so they move. Fast: they sample one frame of this renderer's own copy - the picture this renderer drew before the animated-texture path existed.
wgpu_mc.option.dump_frames.tooltip: Write out the next N frames the renderer presents, as raw files under wgpu-frames, and zero for none. One frame rarely settles a flicker - a handful in a row is what says whether it is on every frame or every other one. Turning it to zero and up again asks for another handful.
wgpu_mc.option.host_validation.tooltip: Load the graphics vendor's own validation layer - D3D12's debug layer, Vulkan's validation layer or GL's debug output - which catches what wgpu cannot see: a barrier in the wrong place, a resource used before its GPU work finished. **It does not switch wgpu's own validation on or off**, which runs either way. Off by default.
wgpu_mc.option.gpu_based_validation.tool: Ask the vendor layer to check what the GPU is actually asked to do rather than only the commands that were recorded, which catches mistakes only the hardware can see. The slowest thing here by a wide margin and a development tool, so it is off by default. It needs Host validation.
wgpu_mc.option.shader_debug_info.tooltip: Build the instance with wgpu's DEBUG flag, so the objects it creates carry the information a graphics debugger reads. It validates nothing and costs nothing per draw; with it off a capture names things like texture_47 instead of wgpu-mc block atlas. On by default.
wgpu_mc.option.validate_indirect_calls.t: Check the arguments in an indirect draw buffer before issuing the draw, and turn the draw into a no-op when they are out of bounds. On by default and it should stay on: without it an out-of-bounds indirect argument is undefined behaviour rather than an error, and on D3D12 it would draw terrain from the wrong offsets. What it costs is a check on a handful of integers per indirect call, not per section.
wgpu_mc.option.discard_backend_labels.to: Do not pass the labels this renderer gives its objects down to the graphics backend, which saves a string lookup and a driver call each time one is created. Off by default, because what the names buy is that a driver's validation error and a graphics debugger both say wgpu-mc section arena instead of a handle.
wgpu_mc.option.allow_noncompliant_adapte: Allow wgpu to offer an adapter whose driver does not meet the graphics API's own requirements - in practice a Vulkan driver reporting a compliance version of 0. Off by default: it is an escape hatch for a machine where nothing else is offered. With it off and no compliant adapter, the game shows its no-supported-backend screen.
wgpu_mc.option.logging.tooltip: Write the renderer's diagnostic log lines: each pipeline the first time it is used, the binding plan it resolves names against, each render pass with its draw count, and the counters once a second. Off by default, because it is a line per pipeline on top of a line per second. It is a log switch only - the frame and texture files are Diagnostics above.
wgpu_mc.option.diagnostics.tooltip: Let the renderer write its dumps out as files: the frame the game is showing, the textures it is showing it with, and a sprite atlas. The dump itself is still asked for by a wgpu-dump-now file in the run directory, because a dump is about one specific frame. A diagnostic session is usually this and Logging together.
wgpu_mc.option.upload_report.tooltip: Report what the renderer's buffer uploads did: every mapped write with the first integers it carried, whether the bytes actually arrived - checked by reading them back from the GPU - and the staging totals. The switch to turn on when an upload is suspected of not landing. Off by default, and a line per upload.
wgpu_mc.option.dump_shaders.tooltip: Write the preprocessed GLSL that actually reaches the shader compiler into wgpu-shaders/. What naga sees is not the source Minecraft handed over, and this is the only place that shows which step went wrong.
wgpu_mc.option.binding_verbosity.tooltip: Report the state of bind groups and range slices.
wgpu_mc.option.gpu_timestamps.tooltip: Write a timestamp at the start of the frame's first submission and the end of its last, for the GPU's own measure of the frame. Printed with the rendering statistics, and it costs extra time.
wgpu_mc.option.pix_capture.tooltip: (DirectX only.) Load PIX's capture libraries into the game so PIX can attach to it, or launch it, for a GPU or timing capture. The libraries have to be loaded before the D3D12 device is created; a timing capture needs administrator rights and its database is very large and very expensive.
wgpu_mc.option.section_timing.tooltip: Time the section feed phase by phase and report the averages on the F3 screen, which is what answers "what does one section rebuild cost, and which part of it". Off by default: it is a clock read per phase per section.
wgpu_mc.option.trace_dynamic_offsets.too: Log every draw's binding plan, each binding in slot order with the offset that travels with it, and the key the bind group cache was asked for. Very loud, and it costs CPU time to write.
wgpu_mc.option.bind_group_cache.tooltip: Reuse bind groups between draws that bind the same resources at different offsets, rather than creating one per draw. On by default; turning it off is how the cache is ruled in or out as the cause of a difference.
wgpu_mc.option.dynamic_offsets.tooltip: Bind uniform buffers with an offset instead of baking the offset into the bind group. On by default, and it is what makes the bind group cache worth having; off is what the renderer did before dynamic offsets existed.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_indirect.tooltip:
Draw the terrain's sections with batched indirect draws - one call per run of sections that share an arena - instead of one call per section. **Both paths are meant to draw the same picture**, so this switch answers "did the batching break something".

**Off by default**: the picture is meant to be identical either way, and the path that is not being measured should not be the one the frame goes through. Turning it on is how the two are compared.

It is forced off where it cannot be worth anything, with the reason in the log. **DirectX 12 never gets it: the call is broken in wgpu's DX12 backend** - wgpu's implementation, not D3D12 and not the driver, which is why no feature test can find it.
wgpu_mc.option.atlas_base_mip_only: Atlas sampled from its base mip only
wgpu_mc.option.atlas_base_mip_only.toolt: Sample the game's own block atlas from its base mip level only, so a distant animated sprite resolves to a single texel rather than a blend of levels. Off by default: the game animates the whole chain, so no level is staler than any other, and clamping to 0 only makes the animated textures alias. Applying it rebuilds the graph.
wgpu_mc.option.game_atlas_blend_mips: Blend the game atlas' mip levels
wgpu_mc.option.game_atlas_blend_mips.too:
Whether the sampler for the game's own block atlas blends between two mip levels or picks one and writes it. On - what the renderer ships, and what vanilla does - blends them; off picks one, which is sharper for a texture that holds still.

**It does not affect the shimmer on flowing water and lava**, which a player measured under both settings. Takes effect on the next frame; applying it rebuilds the graph.
wgpu_mc.option.atlas_lod_bias.tooltip:
Shift the mip level the terrain shaders pick for the block atlases: positive is coarser, negative is finer, and 0 is no shift. A blurry picture that sharpens as this goes negative means the chosen level was too coarse.

It is a measure rather than a picture setting, read per draw, so it takes effect on the next frame - nothing is baked and no pipeline is rebuilt.
wgpu_mc.option.adv_culling.tooltip:
**An experiment that costs frame time rather than saving it**, which is why it sits under Debug. **0**: the game's own occlusion list, which is what this renderer has always obeyed. **1 and up**: this renderer's own direction-aware walk, allowed that many direction changes before a section is dropped - but the walk recomputes an answer the game builds and hands over every frame anyway, so any value above zero lowers the frame rate.

Measured on the frame thread, per frame: about 2 ms at render distance 16 and 8 ms at 32, on top of everything else the frame does. What it reaches is everything the game's own list has that this renderer's frustum would draw anyway, minus about 0.3%. Kept as a measurement rather than as a setting to turn on - making it pay would mean the walk replacing the game's own graph, which is a different architecture.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_occlusion.tooltip:
Honour the game's own occlusion graph and skip the sections it did not name. On is the faster answer and, while that list is right, the correct one.

It is a switch because the list is a **snapshot**: it is only refilled when the camera has turned by more than two degrees or the graph reports a change. A section it has not caught up with is skipped here while the game's own mesh for it stays suppressed, and a section neither side draws is a 16x16x16 hole. With this off every section the frustum contains is drawn.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_no_cull.tooltip:
Draw every pipeline the render graph builds without back-face culling, so the picture stops depending on the winding at all. This is a diagnostic for a picture that is inside out: with both faces rasterized, "the winding is wrong" and "the depth test keeps the wrong end" stop looking the same.

It is not a mode to play with: every quad gets a second copy, shaded with the far side's lighting. Applying it rebuilds the graph's pipelines.
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_greater_depth: Terrain with the depth test reversed
wgpu_mc.option.terrain_greater_depth.too:
Draw every pipeline the render graph builds with the depth test the opposite way round, so the faces behind are the ones kept. The other half of the pair above, and the other reading of a picture whose front faces are missing.

Depth writes are unchanged - the test is what moved - so the picture is the far side of everything the camera can see through. Applying it rebuilds the graph's pipelines.
wgpu_mc.option.window_mode.tooltip:
How the window fills the screen. **Exclusive** is a real display mode switch, the same thing Minecraft's own Fullscreen does; **Borderless** covers the monitor with no decorations but does not change the display mode, which is what to pick if you alt-tab; **Windowed** is a window.

The game's own fullscreen key (F11 by default) toggles between Windowed and whichever mode is chosen here, so the key keeps working.
wgpu_mc.option.fullscreen_mode.tooltip:
How the window fills the screen. **Exclusive** is a real display mode switch, the same thing Minecraft's own Fullscreen does; **Borderless** covers the monitor with no decorations but does not change the display mode, which is what to pick if you alt-tab; **Off** is a window.

The game's own fullscreen key (F11 by default) toggles between Off and whichever mode is chosen here, so the key keeps working.
